claim: The Sec system is the main pathway for protein secretion in all forms of life.
source: The Sec system is the main pathway for protein secretion in all forms of life.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the Sec system's role in protein secretion across different organisms.

claim: SecYEG is a hetero-trimeric membrane protein complex in the plasma membrane of prokaryotes.
source: At the translocon core is a hetero-trimeric membrane protein complex – SecYEG in the plasma membrane of prokaryotes and Sec61αγβ in the ER of eukaryotes – which forms a protein channel across the membrane (Ito et al., 1983; Brundage et al., 1990; Görlich et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research establishing the structure and location of SecYEG.

claim: Sec61αγβ is the translocon complex in the ER of eukaryotes.
source: At the translocon core is a hetero-trimeric membrane protein complex – SecYEG in the plasma membrane of prokaryotes and Sec61αγβ in the ER of eukaryotes – which forms a protein channel across the membrane (Ito et al., 1983; Brundage et al., 1990; Görlich et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The translocon forms a protein channel across the membrane.
source: At the translocon core is a hetero-trimeric membrane protein complex – SecYEG in the plasma membrane of prokaryotes and Sec61αγβ in the ER of eukaryotes – which forms a protein channel across the membrane (Ito et al., 1983; Brundage et al., 1990; Görlich et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pre-protein substrates with an N-terminal signal sequence are targeted to the translocon in an unfolded state.
source: Pre-protein substrates with an N-terminal signal sequence are targeted to the translocon in an unfolded state (Arkowitz et al., 1993), whereupon they are threaded across (secretion) or transferred laterally into the membrane (insertion).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In prokaryotes, secretion is mostly post-translational.
source: In prokaryotes, secretion is mostly post-translational (Hartl et al., 1990): substrates are recognised by the cytosolic ATPase SecA (Lill et al., 1989), which targets them to SecYEG and then drives them through the protein channel using energy derived from ATP binding and hydrolysis, and the trans-membrane proton motive force (PMF) (Brundage et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Substrates are recognised by the cytosolic ATPase SecA.
source: In prokaryotes, secretion is mostly post-translational (Hartl et al., 1990): substrates are recognised by the cytosolic ATPase SecA (Lill et al., 1989), which targets them to SecYEG and then drives them through the protein channel using energy derived from ATP binding and hydrolysis, and the trans-membrane proton motive force (PMF) (Brundage et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: SecA targets substrates to SecYEG and drives them through the protein channel using energy derived from ATP binding and hydrolysis, and the trans-membrane proton motive force (PMF).
source: In prokaryotes, secretion is mostly post-translational (Hartl et al., 1990): substrates are recognised by the cytosolic ATPase SecA (Lill et al., 1989), which targets them to SecYEG and then drives them through the protein channel using energy derived from ATP binding and hydrolysis, and the trans-membrane proton motive force (PMF) (Brundage et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SecY consists of ten trans-membrane helices (TMs).
source: SecY consists of ten trans-membrane helices (TMs), which form a 'clamshell' structure in the membrane, with five TMs on either side of the central protein channel, blocked by a 'plug' and a seal comprising six hydrophobic side chains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data from the cited crystal structure.

claim: SecY forms a 'clamshell' structure in the membrane, with five TMs on either side of the central protein channel.
source: SecY consists of ten trans-membrane helices (TMs), which form a 'clamshell' structure in the membrane, with five TMs on either side of the central protein channel, blocked by a 'plug' and a seal comprising six hydrophobic side chains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data.

claim: The central protein channel is blocked by a 'plug' and a seal comprising six hydrophobic side chains.
source: SecY consists of ten trans-membrane helices (TMs), which form a 'clamshell' structure in the membrane, with five TMs on either side of the central protein channel, blocked by a 'plug' and a seal comprising six hydrophobic side chains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data.

claim: SecE reinforces the SecY conformation on one side.
source: This conformation is reinforced on one side by SecE, while on the opposite side a lateral gate (LG) connects the central protein-conducting channel to the lipid bilayer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data.

claim: A lateral gate (LG) connects the central protein-conducting channel to the lipid bilayer.
source: This conformation is reinforced on one side by SecE, while on the opposite side a lateral gate (LG) connects the central protein-conducting channel to the lipid bilayer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and is based on structural data.

claim: Opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate passage of secretory proteins through the central channel across the membrane.
source: Thus, opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate passage of secretory proteins through the central channel across the membrane, as well as the partitioning of membrane proteins via the LG into the bilayer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of the clamshell opening.

claim: Opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate the partitioning of membrane proteins via the LG into the bilayer.
source: Thus, opening of the 'clamshell' could facilitate passage of secretory proteins through the central channel across the membrane, as well as the partitioning of membrane proteins via the LG into the bilayer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of the clamshell opening.

claim: SecA is a cytoplasmic ATPase that drives protein translocation through SecYEG.
source: SecA is a cytoplasmic ATPase that drives protein translocation through SecYEG (Lill et al., 1989; Brundage et al., 1990; Akimaru et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ATP turnover cycle of SecA is directly coupled to protein translocation.
source: The ATP turnover cycle of SecA is directly coupled to protein translocation (Economou and Wickner, 1994; Karamanou et al., 1999), but as yet the mechanism by which this is accomplished is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mechanism by which ATP turnover is coupled to protein translocation is unclear.
source: The ATP turnover cycle of SecA is directly coupled to protein translocation (Economou and Wickner, 1994; Karamanou et al., 1999), but as yet the mechanism by which this is accomplished is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: SecA consists of two RecA-like nucleotide binding domains (NBD1 and NBD2), which together form the nucleotide-binding site (NBS).
source: Structural studies have revealed that SecA consists of two RecA-like nucleotide binding domains (NBD1 and NBD2), which together form the nucleotide-binding site (NBS) (Hunt et al., 2002) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous structural studies and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: A 'two-helix finger' (2HF) is at the SecY binding interface.
source: A 'two-helix finger' (2HF), at the SecY binding interface (Zimmer et al., 2008), and a pre-protein cross-linking domain (PPXD) both make contacts with the translocating polypeptide (Bauer and Rapoport, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The 2HF and PPXD both make contacts with the translocating polypeptide.
source: A 'two-helix finger' (2HF), at the SecY binding interface (Zimmer et al., 2008), and a pre-protein cross-linking domain (PPXD) both make contacts with the translocating polypeptide (Bauer and Rapoport, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SecY and SecA interact tightly, with the 2HF from SecA protruding into the SecY channel.
source: SecY and SecA interact tightly, with the 2HF from SecA protruding into the SecY channel, and a long loop between TMs 6–7 of SecY buried inside SecA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on the crystal structure of the SecYEG-SecA complex and is supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: A long loop between TMs 6–7 of SecY is buried inside SecA.
source: SecY and SecA interact tightly, with the 2HF from SecA protruding into the SecY channel, and a long loop between TMs 6–7 of SecY buried inside SecA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on the crystal structure of the SecYEG-SecA complex and is supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: A large movement of the PPXD activates the ATPase.
source: In SecA, a large movement of the PPXD activates the ATPase (Gold et al., 2013) and is thought to clamp the substrate in place, while in SecYEG the LG opens, causing a widening of the channel through which translocating substrates pass (Figure 1B) (Zimmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The PPXD movement is thought to clamp the substrate in place.
source: In SecA, a large movement of the PPXD activates the ATPase (Gold et al., 2013) and is thought to clamp the substrate in place, while in SecYEG the LG opens, causing a widening of the channel through which translocating substrates pass (Figure 1B) (Zimmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from structural data.

claim: In SecYEG the LG opens, causing a widening of the channel through which translocating substrates pass.
source: In SecA, a large movement of the PPXD activates the ATPase (Gold et al., 2013) and is thought to clamp the substrate in place, while in SecYEG the LG opens, causing a widening of the channel through which translocating substrates pass (Figure 1B) (Zimmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Complexes were built using the protein and Mg2+ atoms from 3DIN, but with either ADP or ATP in place of ADP-BeFx.
source: To achieve this, complexes were built using the protein and Mg2+ atoms from 3DIN, but with either ADP or ATP in place of ADP-BeFx (Piggot et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the MD simulations.

claim: Five MD simulations of between 0.4–1 µs were run for each state (ATP and ADP).
source: The resultant structures were embedded in a POPC membrane (Ulmschneider and Ulmschneider, 2009) and five MD simulations of between 0.4–1 µs were run for each state (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the MD simulations.

claim: When ADP-BeFx was replaced with ATP, the LG either retained its part-open ('PO') state of about 1.8 nm or widened further to ~2.6 nm forming an open state ('O').
source: When ADP-BeFx was replaced with ATP, the LG either retained its part-open ('PO') state of about 1.8 nm (Figure 2A, middle panel, compare to Figure 2B, lower panel; Figure 2C) or widened further to ~2.6 nm forming an open state ('O'; Figure 2A, lower panel; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the MD simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Substitution of ADP-BeFx with ADP resulted in LG closure in all five simulations to ~1.5 nm ('C').
source: Conversely, substitution of ADP-BeFx with ADP resulted in LG closure in all five simulations to ~1.5 nm ('C'; Figure 2A, upper panel; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the MD simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The closed state closely resembles a previous structure of the resting SecY-complex in the absence of SecA (1RHZ).
source: Remarkably, this closed state closely resembles a previous structure of the resting SecY-complex in the absence of SecA (1RHZ (Van den Berg et al., 2004); Figure 2B, upper panel and Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of MD simulation results with a previously published crystal structure.

claim: Simulations using a different molecular mechanics force field (Amber ff99SB-ILDN) show a similar effect.
source: Note that simulations using a different molecular mechanics force field (Amber ff99SB-ILDN; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) show a similar effect.
evidence: This claim is based on additional MD simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The configuration of helicase motif residues correlates to the open or closed state of the channel.
source: In this system the configuration of these residues correlates to the open or closed state of the channel (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All the ADP and ATP trajectories diverge within the first 10 ns.
source: Nonetheless, the initial opening or closing event is rapid: all the ADP and ATP trajectories diverge within the first 10 ns (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The speed of divergence suggests that the input model represents a high-energy intermediate – probably due to the presence of ADP-BeFx.
source: The speed of this suggests that the input model represents a high-energy intermediate – probably due to the presence of ADP-BeFx.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid divergence observed in the MD simulations.

claim: Donor (Alexa Fluor 488) and acceptor (Alexa Fluor 594) fluorescent probes were attached to a unique cysteine pair flanking the LG (A103 and V353 of Escherichia coli SecY).
source: To test the MD results experimentally, donor (Alexa Fluor 488) and acceptor (Alexa Fluor 594) fluorescent probes were attached to a unique cysteine pair flanking the LG (A103 and V353 of Escherichia coli SecY; Figure 4A; Cβ-Cβ distances 3.4–4.4 nm; the Förster radius, R0, is 6 nm for the chosen dye pair).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for FRET measurements.

claim: The doubly labelled protein (SecY**EG) is active.
source: The doubly labelled protein (hereafter SecY**EG) is active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and limited proteolysis confirms equal labelling on both sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B+C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Limited proteolysis confirms equal labelling on both sites of SecY**EG.
source: The doubly labelled protein (hereafter SecY**EG) is active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and limited proteolysis confirms equal labelling on both sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B+C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B+C.

claim: About 50% of the complexes face outwards after reconstitution into proteo-liposomes (PLs).
source: After reconstitution into proteo-liposomes (PLs), about 50% (as judged by trypsin protection) of the complexes face outwards (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), as has been observed previously for wild-type SecYEG (Mao et al., 2013; Schulze et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous research.

claim: Equilibrium fluorescence measurements of SecY**EG show a decrease in FRET upon binding of SecA.
source: Equilibrium fluorescence measurements of SecY**EG show a decrease in FRET upon binding of SecA (Figure 4B), indicating LG movement – as expected from the crystal structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A further FRET decrease is observed upon addition of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMPPNP, but not ADP.
source: A further FRET decrease is observed upon addition of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue AMPPNP, but not ADP (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The changes in apparent FRET efficiency are not caused by differences in affinity between SecYEG and SecA in different nucleotide states, but rather represent differences in the width of the LG.
source: Titration of SecA into SecY**EG PLs in the presence of either ADP or AMPPNP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) shows that the changes in apparent FRET efficiency are not caused by differences in affinity between SecYEG and SecA in different nucleotide states, but rather represent differences in the width of the LG, i.e. a closure of the LG in the presence of ADP on SecA, some 5 nm away – consistent with the MD results.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and is consistent with MD simulation results.

claim: PLs containing single copies of SecY**EG were tethered to a glass supported bilayer.
source: PLs containing single copies of SecY**EG were tethered to a glass supported bilayer as previously described (Figure 5A) (Deville et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for single molecule FRET measurements.

claim: Particles containing a single FRET pair as judged by sequential single step photobleaching of both dyes were selected for FRET analysis.
source: From time-lapse TIRF images, particles containing a single FRET pair as judged by sequential single step photobleaching of both dyes were selected for FRET analysis (see Materials and methods and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for single molecule FRET measurements.

claim: In the absence of SecA or nucleotide, SecY**EG exists mainly as a single population with an average FRET efficiency (EFRET) of 0.76.
source: In the absence of SecA or nucleotide, SecY**EG exists mainly as a single population with an average FRET efficiency (EFRET) of 0.76 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of SecA causes the open states to become more populated, with the relative populations dependent on which nucleotide is provided.
source: In accord with the ensemble data, addition of SecA causes the open states to become more populated, with the relative populations dependent on which nucleotide is provided (Figure 5C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–G.

claim: At least three components are required to fully describe the histogram distribution with ATP.
source: While a two state model could fit the majority of the distributions (data not shown) both global non-linear fitting (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A) and singular value decomposition (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B) indicate that at least three components are required to fully describe the histogram distribution with ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claim: Three principal states were used to fit the entire dataset: (1) closed, EFRET ~0.76; (2) part-open, EFRET ~0.59; and (3) open, EFRET ~0.45.
source: Therefore three principal states were used to fit the entire dataset: (1) closed, EFRET ~0.76 (red); (2) part-open, EFRET ~0.59 (green); and (3) open, EFRET ~0.45 (blue).
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach for the single molecule FRET experiments.

claim: The difference between the open and closed state is ~0.9 nm.
source: Assuming an R0 of 6 nm, the difference between the open and closed state is ~0.9 nm – consistent with the changes observed across LG by MD (Figure 2C) and those expected from the crystal structures (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of FRET data and is consistent with MD simulations and crystal structures.

claim: In the presence of AMPPNP, the LG occupies mainly the open conformation.
source: These data (Figure 5H) show that in the presence of AMPPNP – which traps the complex in an ATP bound-like state—the LG occupies mainly the open conformation (Figure 5C+H), while with ADP the closed state is more highly populated (Figure 5D+H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, 5H.

claim: With ADP the closed state is more highly populated.
source: These data (Figure 5H) show that in the presence of AMPPNP – which traps the complex in an ATP bound-like state—the LG occupies mainly the open conformation (Figure 5C+H), while with ADP the closed state is more highly populated (Figure 5D+H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D, 5H.

claim: In the presence of ATP, SecY predominantly populates the part-open state.
source: Intriguingly, in the presence of ATP—which under steady-state conditions is rapidly hydrolysed to ADP (Robson et al., 2009)—SecY predominantly populates the part-open state (Figure 5E+H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E, 5H.

claim: Mathematical modelling indicates that the third state cannot be explained by averaging of the two different nucleotide bound forms during data collection.
source: Mathematical modelling indicates that the third state cannot be explained by averaging of the two different nucleotide bound forms during data collection (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C+D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modelling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C+D.

claim: The part-open state most likely represents a true intermediate on the pathway between the closed and open conformations.
source: So, the part-open state most likely represents a true intermediate on the pathway between the closed and open conformations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical modelling and experimental data.

claim: Addition of pOA + ATP to SecY**EG-SecA causes the open state to dominate.
source: Addition of pOA + ATP to SecY**EG-SecA causes the open state to dominate (Figure 5F+H); an effect consolidated by addition of a large excess of SecA and pOA (Figure 5G+H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F, 5G, 5H.

claim: ADP release is strongly accelerated by the presence of pre-protein, such that the open (ATP-bound) state becomes more highly populated.
source: This is consistent with the known properties of the steady-state cycle of SecA: ADP release is strongly accelerated by the presence of pre-protein, such that the open (ATP-bound) state becomes more highly populated (Robson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: No further states of the channel are detected in the presence of the pre-protein.
source: No further states of the channel are detected in the presence of the pre-protein (Figure 5F+G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F, 5G.

claim: Nucleotide occupancy in SecA regulates the opening of the SecY protein-channel and LG.
source: Taken together, the MD and FRET results show that nucleotide occupancy in SecA regulates the opening of the SecY protein-channel and LG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined MD and FRET data.

claim: The MD simulations showed differences in the NBS of SecA, which is more open in the ATP simulations compared to those done with ADP bound.
source: In addition to the LG movement, the MD simulations showed differences in the NBS of SecA, which turns out to be more open in the ATP simulations compared to those done with ADP bound (Figure 6A+B).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of MD simulation data shown in Figure 6A+B.

claim: An open NBS would increase the rate of nucleotide exchange, altering its affinity and turnover.
source: It seems likely that an open NBS would increase the rate of nucleotide exchange, altering its affinity and turnover.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the MD simulation results.

claim: Trapping the LG in a closed position causes a 5-fold reduction in affinity of SecA for AMPPNP.
source: Trapping the LG in a closed position causes a 5-fold reduction in affinity of SecA for AMPPNP (Figure 6C, left), demonstrating that the conformational state of the LG is transmitted to the NBS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The conformational state of the LG is transmitted to the NBS.
source: Trapping the LG in a closed position causes a 5-fold reduction in affinity of SecA for AMPPNP (Figure 6C, left), demonstrating that the conformational state of the LG is transmitted to the NBS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The koff for ADP is slowed by ~50% with a cross-linked LG.
source: We found that the koff is slowed by ~50% with a cross-linked LG (Figure 6D), consistent with the results presented above showing that NBS and LG closure are coordinated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is a two-way communication between SecYEG and SecA over a distance of >5 nm: SecA ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate the aperture of the channel, while LG opening and closing controls the ATP affinity and rate of ADP release from SecA.
source: Together, the results establish the existence of a two-way communication between SecYEG and SecA over a distance of >5 nm: SecA ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate the aperture of the channel, while LG opening and closing controls the ATP affinity and rate of ADP release from SecA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Binding of signal sequence into the LG is known to be an allosteric activator of SecA.
source: Interestingly, binding of signal sequence into the LG is known to be an allosteric activator of SecA (Gouridis et al., 2009; Hizlan et al., 2012): the increase in the turnover of ATP caused by LG opening could provide a basis for this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The increase in the turnover of ATP caused by LG opening could provide a basis for the allosteric activation of SecA by signal sequence binding.
source: Interestingly, binding of signal sequence into the LG is known to be an allosteric activator of SecA (Gouridis et al., 2009; Hizlan et al., 2012): the increase in the turnover of ATP caused by LG opening could provide a basis for this effect.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: The 2HF of SecA is situated directly on the path of pre-proteins as they enter the SecY-channel.
source: The 2HF of SecA is situated directly on the path of pre-proteins as they enter the SecY-channel (Figures 1B and 7A+B), and we have previously shown that perturbing the 2HF by cross-linking to SecY (A795C of SecA cross-linked to K268C of SecY; hereafter SecYxEG-SecA2HF; yellow dotted line in Figure 7B) stimulates the ATPase activity of SecA ~25-fold in PLs (Whitehouse et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on structural data shown in Figures 1B and 7A+B.

claim: Perturbing the 2HF by cross-linking to SecY stimulates the ATPase activity of SecA ~25-fold in PLs.
source: The 2HF of SecA is situated directly on the path of pre-proteins as they enter the SecY-channel (Figures 1B and 7A+B), and we have previously shown that perturbing the 2HF by cross-linking to SecY (A795C of SecA cross-linked to K268C of SecY; hereafter SecYxEG-SecA2HF; yellow dotted line in Figure 7B) stimulates the ATPase activity of SecA ~25-fold in PLs (Whitehouse et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The 2HF might be the sensor that couples the movements of the LG and the NBS.
source: At the time, this observation was surprising; however, in light of the results above, we hypothesised that the 2HF might be the sensor that couples the movements of the LG and the NBS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claim: The 2HF is known to play a crucial role in coupling ATP hydrolysis to translocation.
source: Indeed, the 2HF is known to play a crucial role in coupling ATP hydrolysis to translocation (Erlandson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Covalently cross-linked peptides elicit a significant increase in ADP koff.
source: While the cysteine cross-linking site of SecA itself has no effect on the SecYEG stimulated release of ADP (Figure 7D, compare 'wt + SecYEG ' to 'G793C + SecYEG'), covalently cross-linked peptides elicit a significant increase in ADP koff (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The bulkier peptide, AWCWA, has a greater effect than peptides with smaller residues (AGCGA or AFCFA).
source: The bulkier peptide, AWCWA, has a greater effect than peptides with smaller residues (AGCGA or AFCFA).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental data for different peptides.

claim: Peptides are sensed at the SecY channel entrance, and this information is transmitted back to the NBS.
source: Thus, we conclude that peptides are sensed at the SecY channel entrance, and that this information is transmitted back to the NBS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Both pulling the 2HF away from the channel (with a disulphide bond) and pushing it away (with a bulky peptide) elicit an increase in ADP release.
source: As both pulling the 2HF away from the channel (with a disulphide bond) and pushing it away (with a bulky peptide; Figure 7B) elicit an increase in ADP release, it seems plausible that the 2HF is sensing the passing peptide sterically; the dramatic effects of point mutations in the 2HF (Erlandson et al., 2008; Bauer et al., 2014) are consistent with this interpretation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and is consistent with previous research.

claim: The 2HF is sensing the passing peptide sterically.
source: As both pulling the 2HF away from the channel (with a disulphide bond) and pushing it away (with a bulky peptide; Figure 7B) elicit an increase in ADP release, it seems plausible that the 2HF is sensing the passing peptide sterically; the dramatic effects of point mutations in the 2HF (Erlandson et al., 2008; Bauer et al., 2014) are consistent with this interpretation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the experimental data and is consistent with previous research.

claim: The ease with which a stretch of polypeptide chain passes through the substrate channel depends on the nature of the amino acids in that stretch.
source: Previous studies of translocation by SecYEG-SecA have shown that the ease with which a stretch of polypeptide chain passes through the substrate channel depends on the nature of the amino acids in that stretch (Sato et al., 1997; Bauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Poly-glycine regions diffuse freely and rapidly backwards and forth.
source: For example, poly-glycine regions diffuse freely and rapidly backwards and forth (Bauer et al., 2014), while charged amino acids, especially positively charged, are excluded (Nouwen et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Charged amino acids, especially positively charged, are excluded from the channel.
source: For example, poly-glycine regions diffuse freely and rapidly backwards and forth (Bauer et al., 2014), while charged amino acids, especially positively charged, are excluded (Nouwen et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some combinations of amino acids form secondary structural elements even before they exit the ribosome.
source: It has also been shown that some combinations of amino acids form secondary structural elements even before they exit the ribosome (Hardesty and Kramer, 2001; Lu and Deutsch, 2005), while others remain natively unfolded.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The aperture of the SecY channel is nucleotide-dependent.
source: Given that the aperture of the SecY channel is nucleotide-dependent, we thought it might form a choke point for diffusion of bulky or structured regions of a substrate sequence: in the ADP-bound state, only uncharged, unfolded stretches of polypeptide may pass; whereas the ATP-bound state is less restrictive (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MD and FRET data.

claim: In the ADP-bound state, only uncharged, unfolded stretches of polypeptide may pass; whereas the ATP-bound state is less restrictive.
source: Given that the aperture of the SecY channel is nucleotide-dependent, we thought it might form a choke point for diffusion of bulky or structured regions of a substrate sequence: in the ADP-bound state, only uncharged, unfolded stretches of polypeptide may pass; whereas the ATP-bound state is less restrictive (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claim: All three substrates (AGAGA, AFAFA, AWAWA) crossed the open channel without difficulty.
source: As expected given the dimensions of the open channel (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A), all three substrates crossed without difficulty (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is based on steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: For the closed structure, while AGAGA readily passes through the channel, the larger substrates – especially AWAWA – are substantially retarded.
source: For the closed structure however, while AGAGA readily passes through the channel, the larger substrates – especially AWAWA – are substantially retarded (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is based on steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The closed conformation – favoured by ADP occupied SecA – can permit passage of narrow regions of substrate, but selects against more bulky stretches.
source: This indicates that the closed conformation – favoured by ADP occupied SecA – can permit passage of narrow regions of substrate, but selects against more bulky stretches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the steered MD simulation data.

claim: To allow bulky regions through, the channel would need to open – as occurs when ATP is bound.
source: To allow these bulky regions through, the channel would need to open – as occurs when ATP is bound.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the steered MD simulation data and is consistent with the FRET results.

claim: The most favoured model posits that substrate is pushed through the channel by the 2HF, with ATP providing energy via a power stroke.
source: At present, the most favoured model posits that substrate is pushed through the channel by the 2HF, with ATP providing energy via a power stroke (Erlandson et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the prevailing model in the field at the time of writing, supported by a citation.

claim: Evidence for the power stroke itself is lacking.
source: This model has recently been updated to allow free diffusion of some stretches of less bulky residues (Bauer et al., 2014); however, as we have argued previously (Collinson et al., 2015), evidence for the power stroke itself is lacking.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing model, supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: It is not clear from the structure of SecYEG-SecA where the 2HF would move, and how it could selectively bind and move both hydrophobic and charged regions of substrate.
source: Indeed, it is not clear from the structure of SecYEG-SecA where the 2HF would move, and how it could selectively bind and move both hydrophobic and charged regions of substrate.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing model based on structural considerations.

claim: Immobilisation of the 2HF inside the channel does not prevent translocation.
source: Furthermore, as immobilisation of the 2HF inside the channel does not prevent translocation (Whitehouse et al., 2012), any 'power-stroke' conformational change would have to be extremely subtle.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The SecY channel is predominantly open with ATP bound to SecA and closed with ADP.
source: Here, we have combined all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with single molecule FRET and ensemble biochemical assays to investigate the events that couple the ATPase cycle of SecA with the rest of the complex. Four key observations were made: (i) the SecY channel is predominantly open with ATP bound to SecA and closed with ADP; (ii) the aperture of the channel regulates nucleotide exchange in SecA; (iii) this regulation is sensitive to the size of substrates at the SecYEG channel entrance; and (iv) the closed channel provides a selective barrier against larger substrates.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the combined MD and experimental data.

claim: The aperture of the channel regulates nucleotide exchange in SecA.
source: Here, we have combined all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with single molecule FRET and ensemble biochemical assays to investigate the events that couple the ATPase cycle of SecA with the rest of the complex. Four key observations were made: (i) the SecY channel is predominantly open with ATP bound to SecA and closed with ADP; (ii) the aperture of the channel regulates nucleotide exchange in SecA; (iii) this regulation is sensitive to the size of substrates at the SecYEG channel entrance; and (iv) the closed channel provides a selective barrier against larger substrates.

claim: The regulation of nucleotide exchange is sensitive to the size of substrates at the SecYEG channel entrance.

Four key observations were made: (i) the SecY channel is predominantly open with ATP bound to SecA and closed with ADP; (ii) the aperture of the channel regulates nucleotide exchange in SecA; (iii) this regulation is sensitive to the size of substrates at the SecYEG channel entrance; and (iv) the closed channel provides a selective barrier against larger substrates.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the combined MD and experimental data.

claim: The closed channel provides a selective barrier against larger substrates.
source: Here, we have combined all-atom molecular dynamics simulations with single molecule FRET and ensemble biochemical assays to investigate the events that couple the ATPase cycle of SecA with the rest of the complex. Four key observations were made: (i) the SecY channel is predominantly open with ATP bound to SecA and closed with ADP; (ii) the aperture of the channel regulates nucleotide exchange in SecA; (iii) this regulation is sensitive to the size of substrates at the SecYEG channel entrance; and (iv) the closed channel provides a selective barrier against larger substrates.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the combined MD and experimental data.

claim: The direction of random substrate diffusion (Brownian motion) is biased by the action of the ATPase.
source: In our proposed model (Figure 8 and Movie 1) the direction of random substrate diffusion (Brownian motion [Simon et al., 1992]) is biased by the action of the ATPase.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the combined experimental and simulation data.

claim: In the absence of blockages, the polypeptide diffuses freely backwards and forwards through the closed (ADP-bound) channel.
source: In the absence of blockages, the polypeptide diffuses freely backwards and forwards through the closed (ADP-bound) channel (state (i) in Figure 8).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 8.

claim: When a region of polypeptide that cannot pass through reaches the channel entrance, it triggers nucleotide exchange – probably via the 2HF.
source: When a region of polypeptide that cannot pass through reaches the channel entrance (state (ii) – block region as green circle), it triggers nucleotide exchange – probably via the 2HF (state (iii)).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 8.

claim: Nucleotide exchange causes a brief opening of the channel, allowing the polypeptide to diffuse freely, before ATP is hydrolysed and the channel closes.
source: This causes a brief opening of the channel (iv), allowing the polypeptide to diffuse freely, before ATP is hydrolysed and the channel closes ((ii) or (v) depending on the position of the block).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 8.

claim: Back-diffusion is restricted because bulky regions on the periplasmic side do not trigger nucleotide exchange.
source: Back-diffusion is restricted because bulky regions on the periplasmic side do not trigger nucleotide exchange (vi): the whole scheme therefore acts as a ratchet promoting translocation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 8.

claim: The bias for forward directionality arises because the energy transducing (ATP dependent) step – which resolves channel blockages – happens at the cytosolic, but not the periplasmic, surface.
source: In essence, the bias for forward directionality arises because the energy transducing (ATP dependent) step – which resolves channel blockages – happens at the cytosolic, but not the periplasmic, surface.
evidence: This is an explanation of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The irreversibility of the initiation and completion steps would ensure forward directionality.
source: Moreover, the irreversibility of the initiation and completion steps would ensure forward directionality: once the signal sequence makes contact with the lipid bilayer (McKnight et al., 1991; Hizlan et al., 2012; Corey et al., 2016) it remains firmly fixed there, and is not cleaved off until most or all of the protein has crossed (Josefsson and Randall, 1981).
evidence: This is an explanation of the proposed mechanism, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Once the signal sequence makes contact with the lipid bilayer it remains firmly fixed there.
source: Moreover, the irreversibility of the initiation and completion steps would ensure forward directionality: once the signal sequence makes contact with the lipid bilayer (McKnight et al., 1991; Hizlan et al., 2012; Corey et al., 2016) it remains firmly fixed there, and is not cleaved off until most or all of the protein has crossed (Josefsson and Randall, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The signal sequence is not cleaved off until most or all of the protein has crossed.
source: Moreover, the irreversibility of the initiation and completion steps would ensure forward directionality: once the signal sequence makes contact with the lipid bilayer (McKnight et al., 1991; Hizlan et al., 2012; Corey et al., 2016) it remains firmly fixed there, and is not cleaved off until most or all of the protein has crossed (Josefsson and Randall, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The proposed model retains scope for further acceleration by the PMF, folding, or by the binding of periplasmic chaperones.
source: Moreover, because much of the peptide is diffusing rather than being pushed, the proposed model retains scope for further acceleration by the PMF (Brundage et al., 1990), folding, or by the binding of periplasmic chaperones: these factors would also prevent backsliding, and thereby promote flux towards the periplasmic side of the membrane.
evidence: This is a discussion of the implications of the proposed model, with a citation to previous research.

claim: The PMF, folding, and periplasmic chaperones would prevent backsliding, and thereby promote flux towards the periplasmic side of the membrane.
source: Moreover, because much of the peptide is diffusing rather than being pushed, the proposed model retains scope for further acceleration by the PMF (Brundage et al., 1990), folding, or by the binding of periplasmic chaperones: these factors would also prevent backsliding, and thereby promote flux towards the periplasmic side of the membrane.
evidence: This is a discussion of the implications of the proposed model.

claim: The different open and closed states required for the model are represented in the various structures of the translocon determined in the presence or absence of translocation partners and engaged translocation substrate.
source: The different open and closed states required for the model are represented in the various structures of the translocon determined in the presence or absence of translocation partners and engaged translocation substrate (Van den Berg et al., 2004; Zimmer et al., 2008; Park et al., 2014; Gogala et al., 2014; Pfeffer et al., 2015; Voorhees and Hegde, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous structural studies.

claim: A structure of SecYEG-SecA was very recently determined with a pseudo pre-protein within the channel.
source: Indeed, a structure of SecYEG-SecA was very recently determined with a pseudo pre-protein within the channel (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent structural study.

claim: With a narrow region of polypeptide (Ala-Gly-Gly) in the centre of the channel and ADP-BeFx bound to the NBS, the LG closely resembles that of 3DIN.
source: With a narrow region of polypeptide (Ala-Gly-Gly) in the centre of the channel and ADP-BeFx bound to the NBS, the LG closely resembles that of 3DIN (Zimmer et al., 2008) – or the part-open conformation reported here.
evidence: This is a comparison of a recently published structure with the results of this study.

claim: The pore-ring is packed tightly around the Ala-Gly-Gly sequence, suggesting that with substrate bound, the complex might not reach the fully closed state described here (upon ATP hydrolysis).
source: The pore-ring is packed tightly around this sequence, suggesting (i) that with substrate bound, the complex might not reach the fully closed state described here (upon ATP hydrolysis), and (ii) that further opening (upon ATP binding) would be required to accommodate a larger region of substrate – as we propose here.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with a recently published structure.

claim: Further opening (upon ATP binding) would be required to accommodate a larger region of substrate.
source: The pore-ring is packed tightly around this sequence, suggesting (i) that with substrate bound, the complex might not reach the fully closed state described here (upon ATP hydrolysis), and (ii) that further opening (upon ATP binding) would be required to accommodate a larger region of substrate – as we propose here.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with a recently published structure and is consistent with the proposed model.

claim: The ATP-bound state of SecA binds more tightly to substrate than the ADP-bound state.
source: It has been reported that the ATP-bound state of SecA binds more tightly to substrate than the ADP-bound state (Bauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Differential substrate binding could be evidence of an additional pre-protein clamp in SecA.
source: This could be evidence of an additional pre-protein clamp in SecA (Bauer and Rapoport, 2009), perhaps designed to prevent the (iv) → (ii) transition in Figure 8: such a possibility is not precluded by the data, and would represent a refinement of the model presented here.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible refinement to the proposed model.

claim: Differential substrate binding could form part of a proof-reading mechanism to prevent poorly translocated substrates from clogging and jamming the Sec machinery.
source: Alternately, it could form part of a proof-reading mechanism to prevent poorly translocated substrates from clogging and jamming the Sec machinery (Liang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible alternative explanation, supported by a citation.

claim: Clogging and jamming of the Sec machinery is deleterious to cells, leading to degradation of SecY.
source: This is known to be deleterious to cells, leading to degradation of SecY (van Stelten et al., 2009); SecA has indeed been reported to have unfolding activity (Arkowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SecA has been reported to have unfolding activity.
source: This is known to be deleterious to cells, leading to degradation of SecY (van Stelten et al., 2009); SecA has indeed been reported to have unfolding activity (Arkowitz et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The proposed model accounts for the translocation intermediates sometimes observed at low ATP concentrations.
source: The proposed model (Figure 8 and Video 1) accounts for many previously noted properties of translocation: for example, the translocation intermediates sometimes observed at low ATP concentrations (van der Wolk et al., 1997) could be caused by regions of substrate with particularly high energy barriers to transit.
evidence: This is a discussion of how the proposed model explains previous observations, supported by a citation.

claim: The proposed model would give rise to an approximately linear dependence of translocation rate on substrate length.
source: It would also give rise to an approximately linear dependence of translocation rate on substrate length (Liang et al., 2009) – especially those with repeating sequences (Tomkiewicz et al., 2006) – while giving different rates for substrates with markedly different sequences (Sato et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a discussion of how the proposed model explains previous observations, supported by citations.

claim: ATP-bound SecA is bound tightly to the channel, while the ADP-bound form can be released.
source: Furthermore, the fact that ATP-bound SecA is bound tightly to the channel, while the ADP-bound form can be released (Bauer et al., 2014), makes sense from the perspective of cellular homeostasis and membrane integrity: release of SecA from a wide open SecY channel would allow the leakage of ions and compromise the energy conserving capabilities of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Release of SecA from a wide open SecY channel would allow the leakage of ions and compromise the energy conserving capabilities of the plasma membrane.
source: Furthermore, the fact that ATP-bound SecA is bound tightly to the channel, while the ADP-bound form can be released (Bauer et al., 2014), makes sense from the perspective of cellular homeostasis and membrane integrity: release of SecA from a wide open SecY channel would allow the leakage of ions and compromise the energy conserving capabilities of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the differential binding.

claim: The proposed mechanism resembles a suggested mechanism for the eukaryotic Sec machinery, but with ratcheting from the cytosolic rather than the distal side of the membrane.
source: The above mechanism represents a breakthrough in our understanding of protein export through the ubiquitous Sec complex. It also resembles a suggested mechanism for the eukaryotic Sec machinery (Matlack et al., 1999), but with ratcheting from the cytosolic rather than the distal side of the membrane, which compensates for the absence of ATP in the periplasm.
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously proposed mechanism for the eukaryotic system, supported by a citation.

claim: Regulated constriction of the channel may offer a unifying concept for protein transport more generally, e.g. in mitochondrial and chloroplast protein import.
source: Regulated constriction of the channel, therefore, may offer a unifying concept for protein transport more generally, e.g. in mitochondrial and chloroplast protein import.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Two-way communication between the ATPase NBS and the polymer binding site over distances ranging from 2 to 15 nm has been observed for several molecular motors such as RecA-like helicases and AAA+ dynein.
source: Furthermore, two-way communication between the ATPase NBS and the polymer binding site over distances ranging from 2 to 15 nm has been observed for several molecular motors such as RecA-like helicases (Mancini et al., 2004; Kainov et al., 2008) and AAA+ dynein (Kon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on other molecular motors.

claim: A common mechanism may underlie many other systems responsible for the conversion of chemical energy into directional motion of proteins and nucleic acids.
source: Thus, a common mechanism is emerging that may underlie many other systems responsible for the conversion of chemical energy into directional motion of proteins and nucleic acids.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the proposed mechanism.

claim: ATP binding by SecA causes opening of the SecY-channel at long range.
source: We show that ATP binding by SecA causes opening of the SecY-channel at long range, while substrates at the SecY-channel entrance feed back to regulate nucleotide exchange by SecA.
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the combined MD and experimental data.

claim: This two-way communication suggests a new, unifying 'Brownian ratchet' mechanism, whereby ATP binding and hydrolysis bias the direction of polypeptide diffusion.
source: This two-way communication suggests a new, unifying 'Brownian ratchet' mechanism, whereby ATP binding and hydrolysis bias the direction of polypeptide diffusion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the combined experimental and simulation data.

claim: The model represents a solution to the problem of transporting inherently variable substrates such as polypeptides.
source: The model represents a solution to the problem of transporting inherently variable substrates such as polypeptides, and may underlie mechanisms of other motors that translocate proteins and nucleic acids.
